content: There is increasing interest in utilizing schools as platforms for immunization and immunization screening, particularly for older children receiving routine vaccines such as DTP, Td, or the second dose of the measles vaccine. This approach is becoming more promising due to rising school enrollment rates, especially in low-income countries. Schools provide an excellent opportunity to integrate vaccine delivery with other health and nutrition interventions aimed at reducing vaccine-preventable diseases (VPDs) and improving overall population health. For instance, HPV vaccination can be combined with health education to prevent tobacco use, which serves as a primary cancer prevention strategy. Similarly, information on healthy diets can be provided to prevent overweight, obesity, and diet-related non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Schools can also serve as venues to distribute puberty and menstruation education booklets or iron/folic acid supplements to adolescents. Additionally, linking HPV vaccine delivery with other health interventions, such as deworming, can enhance the coverage of these interventions while reducing overall delivery costs. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a School Vaccination Readiness Assessment Tool to evaluate a country’s preparedness for implementing school-based vaccination programs. This tool is part of a broader strategy to identify opportunities across the life course to deliver effective interventions for cervical cancer prevention and control, leveraging the natural history of the disease. The Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Pneumonia and Diarrhoea (GAPPD), launched by WHO and UNICEF in 2013, proposes an integrated framework of key interventions to prevent and treat childhood pneumonia and diarrhea. These include vaccines (e.g., pertussis, measles, Haemophilus influenzae type b, pneumococcal conjugate, and rotavirus), handwashing with soap, exclusive breastfeeding for six months, vitamin A supplementation, and appropriate treatment. However, these interventions are not always promoted together to maximize their benefits. GAPPD emphasizes the need to integrate activities, capture synergies, and improve efficiency. Sudan, for example, introduced the rotavirus vaccine in 2011 with Gavi support, along with the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) and the meningitis A vaccine (MenA). These efforts have strengthened primary healthcare and equity. Despite progress, challenges remain, such as weak community-based disease surveillance among internally displaced persons and refugees due to ongoing conflict. Sudan has implemented a weekly case-based VPD surveillance system and introduced reporting on adverse events following immunization and intussusception. Water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) improvements are critical for reducing diseases like rotavirus, cholera, and typhoid. WHO and UNICEF have committed to achieving universal WASH access in healthcare facilities by 2030. The WASH FIT tool has been implemented in 15 countries, providing a mechanism for sustained change. However, more rigorous monitoring and integration with broader health system strengthening efforts are needed. In Nepal, a novel approach integrated hygiene promotion into the routine immunization program in four pilot districts. This initiative targeted mothers and caregivers of infants and trained female community health volunteers. Hygiene promotion activities, such as storytelling, handwashing rituals, and competitions, were conducted at immunization clinics. The program significantly improved hygiene behaviors, increased immunization coverage, reduced vaccine wastage, and reached previously underserved populations. Plans are underway to scale this approach nationwide. The Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI), launched by WHO and UNICEF in 1995, combines prevention and treatment of common childhood illnesses into simple guidelines for health workers. IMCI training includes assessing a child’s vaccination status and providing necessary immunizations. Regular reinforcement of these practices is essential to ensure sustained improvements in immunization coverage and child health outcomes.
